description: Somos FOCUS, un equipo de adolescentes—Solange, Lizmarie, Ian y Neyfer que queria hacer algo completamente nuevo. Entramos al NASA Space Apps Challenge sin experiencia previa en el algo relacionado con el espacio y sabiendo muy poco de programación, pero con muchísimas ganas de aprender.
summary: We created IGNIS to tackle the "Flame in Freefall" challenge because we believe space fire safety data shouldn't be locked away in complicated and long spreadsheets. Built with Python, IGNIS is a web control panel that gathers, compares, and breaks down microgravity combustion data extracted from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository.To make the experience truly accessible and personal, we also built in an AI chatbot so users can just ask questions and get clear, tailored answers right away, turning the data into something anyone could easily explore. Our main goal is giving everyone, from students to professors and professionals the power to explore how fire behaves in space by making NASA’s real experimental data easy to visualize and question. As a team, we chose this challenge because we recognize the importance of  understanding fire in space for future space exploration. We aim to speed up fire safety research and support safer life in orbit.
details:
What it Does & How it Works.

IGNIS is an experimental web platform built around "Reasearch-to-Safety Intelligence" that collects, analyzes, and presents NASA'S microgravity combustion data. Insted of forcing users to dig through raw files, the interface organize complex researche into dedicated, interactive workspace windows, including the Mission Dashboard (Which tracks real-time backend status, indexed documents, and research fragments), Research Intelligence, Combustion Explores, Habitat Safety, Next-Gen Safety and more features. Alongside these visual tools, IGNIS features a built-in AI assistant in the bottom corner of the workspace. While the platform is an experimental project and the chatbot is a trial version in progress and only works local for now, it allow users to ask specific questions about fire behavior in space and receive instant, evidence-informed answers.

Key Benefits.

Decades of NASA microgravity fire research are currently stored across dense, complicated spreadsheets and technical papers that take hours to navigate and compare. IGNIS solves this bottleneck by turning the extense results of experimental data into an intuitive, conversational experiences. It saves researchers, students, and educators valuable time by letting them spot patterns, monitor indexed scientific documents, and pull clear insights in seconds, making critical fire safety knowledge accesible to everyone regardless of their technical background.

Intended Impact.

As humanity prepares to return to the Moon and push forward to Mars, understanding how flames behave is reduced gravity is vital for keeping astronauts safe. Our intended impact to bridge the gap between orbital combustion science and practical space-habitat safety. By removing the technical barriers surrounding NASA's open research, IGNIS empowers the next generation of students, professors, and aerospace professionals to buil safer spacecraft and habitats.

Creativity & Innovation.

Rather than treating orbital research like a static archive, our creative approach lets users literally talk to data. Combining clean mission control with interactive exploration modules and a local voice-and-text AI transforms dry telemetry into dynamic conversation. Futhermore, as a team of high school students who entered this challenge with almost no prior coding or space science experiences, we designed the exact kind of intuitive, stress-free interface we wished existed when we first openend NASA's archives.

Factors Considered.

When developing IGNIS, our team prioritized scientific accuracy, user accessibility, and long term scalability:

  • Verified Data: We grounded the system in real experimental results archived in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository so every insight is backed by science.
  • Accessibility: We structured the workspace so both seasoned researchers and curious high school students can navigate complex fire behavior effortlessly.
  • Future Scalability: We engineered IGNIS to grow alongdide active space researche, with plan to continuosly integrate new datasets as ongoing NASA combustion experiments like SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) get published to the NASA database.

Technical Stack & Development Tools.

To bring this version to life, our team built IGNIS using the following tools:

  • Programming Languages: We used Python for backend development and data processing alongside JavaScript, CSS, and HTML for the interactive visual desing, animations, and web structure.
  • Frameworks and Libraries: We relied on React and Lucide React for the user experience and iconography, FastAPI and Uvicorn to run our backend services, and ChromaDB for vector-based storage of scientific document segments.
  • Artificial Intelligence Tools: We used Ollama running the Llama 3.2 model locally to power the IGNIS assistant, supported by Claude and ChatGPT for research, planning, code generation and review.
  • Development Tools: Our workflow and environments were managed through Visual Studio Code, Git, Node.js, npm.
  • Scientific Processing Technologies: We connected the frontend and backend via REST API and JSON, utilizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), embeddings, and vector search to retrieve relevant research fragments and generate accurate answers directly from NASA's findings.
dataRefs: A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science
